main.claim: Paste a meeting transcript or your notes, or upload a recording, and get clean minutes: a summary, key decisions, action items with owners and deadlines when they are mentioned, and open questions. Free, no account needed.

sections.heading: How to generate meeting minutes
sections.body:
Open the [meeting minutes generator](https://meeting-minutes.lazur.app/) and follow these steps.

1. Paste a transcript or your notes into the text box. Or upload a recording, as an audio or video file of up to 15 MB.
2. Run the generator and wait a few seconds for the draft.
3. Read the draft against the meeting, and correct anything that is wrong.
4. Copy the minutes with one click and paste them into your document or email.

You can use the generator for a team meeting, a client call or a board discussion. The layout is the same each time, so the minutes from one meeting are easy to compare with the next.

sections.heading: What the minutes contain
sections.body:
Every draft uses the same four parts.

- **Summary:** two or three lines on what the meeting covered.
- **Key decisions:** what the group agreed to.
- **Action items:** each task, with its owner and deadline if the meeting named them.
- **Open questions:** points that were raised but not settled.

The summary is the part people read first, so keep it short. The decisions and action items are the part people act on, so check those first.

sections.heading: Owners and dates: what the generator will not add
sections.body:
The generator does not invent names or dates. If nobody said who owns a task, the action item comes out without an owner. If no deadline was mentioned, there is no deadline. That is deliberate, because a made-up owner or date sends the wrong person a task.

Before you share the minutes, add any missing owners yourself, and compare every decision and date with what was said. A meeting with clear owners gives you complete action items. A meeting with vague ones gives you gaps you need to fill.

sections.heading: Transcript, notes or recording
sections.body:
Use a transcript when you have one. You can read it before you run the generator, and you can fix names or terms that the transcription got wrong, so those mistakes do not carry into the minutes.

If you have no transcript, upload the recording. Audio files and video files both work. Zoom saves its cloud recordings as MP4 or M4A files, which you can upload directly, as listed in [Zoom's recording file formats article](https://support.zoom.com/hc/en/article?id=zm_kb&sysparm_article=KB0064394).

If you only have rough notes, paste them in. The generator arranges them into the same four parts.

sections.heading: Limits and the free plan
sections.body:
The generator is free. You get 3 runs a day, and after you leave an email you get 3 more. You do not need an account to start.

Files must be 15 MB or smaller. A long meeting recorded as video can pass that limit. An audio-only file is usually much smaller, so save or export the audio on its own if your app lets you. If the file is still too big, split the recording at a natural break, such as the end of an agenda item, and run each part. Then join the minutes into one document.

The generator runs on Lazur's servers and uses Google's Gemini model to write the minutes. Do not paste anything you are not allowed to share with that kind of service.

sections.heading: Dictating notes on a Mac
sections.body: If you write up notes after every meeting, dictation can be faster than typing. On a Mac, Lazur lets you hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

sections.heading: How to turn a recording into minutes
sections.body:
Open the [recording version of the generator](https://meeting-minutes.lazur.app/from-recording) and follow these steps.

1. Upload the recording as an audio or video file. The limit is 15 MB.
2. Wait a few seconds while the minutes are written.
3. Read the draft and listen to the parts where a decision or deadline was agreed.
4. Copy the minutes with one click.

Audio files, such as M4A, and video files, such as MP4, both work. Zoom saves cloud recordings as MP4 or M4A files, so you can upload the file you download from Zoom directly. Zoom's [recording file formats article](https://support.zoom.com/hc/en/article?id=zm_kb&sysparm_article=KB0064394) lists the formats it uses.

sections.heading: Keep the recording under 15 MB
sections.body:
A file over 15 MB will not upload. A long video often passes that limit, so save the audio on its own if your app offers that option. Audio-only files are usually much smaller than the same meeting as video. Check the file size in your file manager before you upload, so you know whether to save the audio or split the file first. A quick check now saves a failed upload later.

If the file is still too big, cut it into parts at a natural break, such as the end of an agenda item. Run the generator on each part. Then join the minutes into one document, and remove any action item that appears twice.

sections.heading: What a recording can and cannot give you
sections.body:
The minutes come from what the recording sounds like. Crosstalk, a loud room, a bad connection or a speaker far from the mic all lower the quality of the draft. A short clip with clear speech gives you a cleaner result than a long, noisy one.

Say each action item out loud in the meeting, with the owner and the date. A line such as "Sam will send the revised plan by Friday" gives the draft a clear owner and deadline, so nothing is left blank. Tasks that were only hinted at tend to come out with gaps.

Listen to the parts where something was decided. Check each owner and each date against the recording. The generator does not invent names or dates, so a task that nobody assigned will come out without an owner, and you need to add it yourself.

sections.heading: When to paste a transcript instead
sections.body:
If your meeting app or transcription tool already made a transcript, paste that instead of the recording. A transcript is smaller, so it avoids the 15 MB limit, and you can read it and fix wrong names before you run the generator.

The same four parts come out either way: a summary, key decisions, action items and open questions.

faq.q: Can AI generate meeting minutes from a recording?
faq.a: Yes. Upload an audio or video file of up to 15 MB to the meeting minutes generator, and it writes minutes with a summary, key decisions, action items and open questions. Owners and deadlines appear only when the recording names them. Copy the result with one click.

faq.q: What file types can I upload?
faq.a: The generator accepts audio files, such as M4A, and video files, such as MP4. Each file must be 15 MB or smaller. If a file is larger, save the audio on its own or cut the recording into parts and run each part separately.

faq.q: Can I make minutes from a Zoom recording?
faq.a: Yes, if the file is 15 MB or smaller. Zoom saves cloud recordings as MP4 or M4A files. Download the recording from Zoom, then upload it to the generator. If your file is larger than 15 MB, split it first.

faq.q: Do I need an account to upload a recording?
faq.a: No. The free plan gives you 3 runs a day, and you get 3 more after you leave an email. You do not need an account to start, so you can try it with a short clip first.

sections.heading: Clean up the transcript first
sections.body:
Before you paste, delete any lines that are not part of the meeting, such as chat before the call started or a side conversation that was not on the agenda. Fewer off-topic lines means a clearer summary.

Then check the names. A name spelled wrong in the transcript will be spelled wrong in the minutes, so fix every name and any product or project term that the transcription got wrong. Ten minutes of this work saves a correction email later.

Keep each speaker's name the same throughout. If one line says Dana and another says Dana Reyes, the minutes may treat them as two people. Pick the form your team uses and apply it everywhere.

sections.heading: What each part of the minutes holds
sections.body:
The minutes have four parts, and each one answers a different question.

- **Summary:** two or three lines on what the meeting was about and how it ended.
- **Key decisions:** what the group agreed, in plain words.
- **Action items:** the task, its owner and its deadline. The owner and deadline appear only when the transcript names them.
- **Open questions:** the points that were raised but not settled.

Minutes record decisions and the reasons for them. They do not need every sentence that was said, so the summary and decisions are the parts to read most closely.

sections.heading: Check the draft before you share it
sections.body:
The generator works from your text, so the draft is only as accurate as the transcript. Read each decision against the transcript. Look at each action item and confirm the owner is the right person.

If an owner or a date is missing, the transcript did not give one. Add it yourself, from your memory of the meeting or from the person who ran it, rather than guessing.

Read the open questions too. If a question in the draft was settled during the meeting, the answer is in the transcript, so search for it and add it to the decisions. Once the draft matches the transcript, copy it into the document your team uses and send it to the people who need to act.

pages.description: Learn how to make minutes for a meeting: what to record before, during and after, and how to turn your notes into a clean draft with a free tool.
pages.h1: How to make minutes for a meeting
pages.claim: Make minutes in three stages: prepare with the agenda, record decisions and owned action items during the meeting, then write them up plainly and send them quickly. Or paste your notes into a free generator.

sections.heading: Before the meeting
sections.body:
Read the agenda and any papers that go with it. Knowing the context lets you spot the points that matter, so you can write them down clearly.

Set up a simple page with the date, the time, the place and a list of who is expected. Leave room under each agenda item for decisions and tasks. That way you are not searching through a page of notes after the meeting.

sections.heading: During the meeting
sections.body:
Record what was said and decided, not what you think about it. Write the outcome of each agenda item, the reason for any decision, and any votes. Leave out long quotes and side conversations.

Whenever someone agrees to do something, write it down as an action item with the person's name and a deadline. If no deadline is set, write that down too, so the gap is visible. A line such as "The team approved the budget for the new website" tells the reader what happened without a story.

If the meeting runs long, take a short break in your notes at each new agenda item. Write the item name first, then the outcome. That keeps the notes in agenda order, which is the order most readers expect.

sections.heading: After the meeting
sections.body:
Turn your notes into full sentences in plain, direct language. Keep each point short. Check every name and date against your notes, and check that each action item has an owner.

Send the minutes while the meeting is still fresh, so people can correct any mistake and start on their tasks. Keep a copy in the same place each time, so the next person can find it.

If the same point appears in several meetings, carry it forward as an open question until someone records a decision. Repeated tasks with no owner are often the first sign that a meeting needs a clear chair, so note that for the next agenda.

sections.heading: Write the draft faster with a generator
sections.body:
If your notes are rough, a generator can arrange them into minutes for you. Open the [meeting minutes generator](https://meeting-minutes.lazur.app/make) and paste your notes into the text box. It writes a summary, key decisions, action items and open questions.

Action items show an owner and deadline only when your notes name them. The generator does not invent names or dates, so check the draft against your notes before you share it. The generator is free, with 3 runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email.

For a meeting you will need to write up again next week, keep the same sections each time. The same four parts in the same order make the next set of minutes quicker to write and easier for readers to scan.

faq.q: How do I write good minutes of a meeting?
faq.a: Keep them short, factual and neutral. Record the date, who attended, each decision and each action item with its owner and deadline. Leave out long quotes and your own opinions. Read the draft against your notes before you send it.

faq.q: What should the minutes of a meeting include?
faq.a: Usually the date, time and place, who attended, the main points discussed, decisions and any votes, and action items with an owner and a deadline. Add open questions for any point that was left unresolved, so the next meeting picks it up.

faq.q: Can I make minutes from my notes automatically?
faq.a: Yes. Paste your rough notes into the meeting minutes generator and it arranges them into a summary, key decisions, action items and open questions. It does not invent names or dates. Check the draft against your notes, then copy it with one click.
